title: The Elder and the Chosen Lady
subtitle: 2 John 1:1–3
description: A title instead of a name: the elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, loved in a truth that abides forever, with grace, mercy, and peace stated as what will be with us.
paragraphs: The whole letter fits on one page, and it signs itself with a title instead of a name: “The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth.” The elder is all he calls himself, an old man in the faith writing with the weight of years and no need to argue his standing. The address is a household: a chosen lady and her children. And the love he declares for them has a location, in the truth, as if love had an address and the truth were it. In the first letter of this group the truth was what the witnesses testified; in this shortest letter the truth is the country the love lives in.

The sentence runs on past its own break to widen the love beyond the writer: “and not I alone, but also all who know the truth,” and then it gives the reason, and the reason is the truth's own permanence: “because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever:” Abides is the word this writer cannot leave alone; it was the master word of the long letter and it is the ground here. The lady and her children are loved by everyone who knows the truth because the truth itself is a resident, abiding in the elder and the knowers alike, and its lease is forever. People pass; households scatter; the truth that abides will be with us forever, and the love built on it is built on the one thing in the letter that cannot leave.

The greeting that follows is not phrased as a wish, and the difference is worth keeping. “Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love.” Will be with us: a statement, carrying the certainty of the truth it rests on. Its source is double-named, God the Father and Jesus Christ, here given the title the Son of the Father, and its atmosphere is the letter's twin rails in one phrase, in truth and love. Three gifts, two givers named as one source, and the two words that will govern every verse that follows.

Two things about this letter the telling states plainly once, here. The elder never names himself; tradition has long ascribed the letter to John the apostle, and that ascription is named as tradition, with his authority left where the letter leaves it, on the elder's own voice and the truth he is known by. And the chosen lady has been read two ways by Christians for a very long time, as a woman and her household, and as a congregation pictured as a lady with her children; the letter does not settle the reading, and the telling takes no side, carrying her as he addresses her. This book stands in the undated group of this series, with no date given and none invented. The elect sister of the closing verse belongs to the same household of faith, whichever reading a person takes, and she will greet the lady at the letter's end.

So the shortest letter in this group opens with its whole worldview in three verses: an elder, a household, love located in a truth that abides forever, and gifts that will be with us in truth and love. What follows is the elder's joy and his single request, and both concern walking: children found walking in the truth, and a commandment as old as the beginning, that we love one another.

title: Walking in Truth and Love
subtitle: 2 John 1:4–6
description: Joy over children found walking in the truth, and the letter's one request: not a new commandment, but the old one from the beginning, that we love one another.
paragraphs: The elder's first report is joy, and the joy has a specific cause: “I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us.” Found, as if the news reached him or the visit showed him, and walking, the long letter's test-word for a life in motion. The truth is not only known in this household; it is being walked in, by her children, in obedience to a command that came from the Father. One word in the sentence is sober, and the telling does not hurry past it: some of your children. Not all are named in the joy. The letter does not say what the others are doing, and no explanation is invented for them; the joy over the walking ones and the silence over the rest stand side by side, the way they stand in many households.

Then comes the letter's one request, and it is framed as the opposite of news. The verse breaks around its own clarification, so the telling carries it as written: “And now I urge you, dear lady” and then the clarification itself, “not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning,” and then the request, “that we love one another.” Urge is a strong word from an elder to a lady, and he softens it with dear and with the commandment's age. He is not importing an idea. He is reminding her of the first thing they ever heard, the message that stood at the beginning of the long letter too: love one another. The request's humility is its authority; nothing here is the elder's invention.

The commandment's age is the point he keeps circling. From the beginning is this writer's signature phrase for it, and love, in his handling, is never a mood that descends. The next verse defines it by motion: “And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love.” Love is walking according to the commandments, and the commandment is walking in love: the sentence is a circle and it is meant to be, each side defining the other so neither can be had alone. Feeling without obedience is not what he calls love, and obedience without love is not what he calls walking.

So the lady's household stands in three verses exactly where the long letter's readers stood: truth to walk in, love to walk by, and both of them old. Nothing in the elder's request would prepare a reader for severity, and yet severity is where the letter goes next, because the walking household is not the only traffic on the road. Deceivers have gone out into the same world her children walk in, and the elder's tone changes from urging to warning in a single verse.

title: Do Not Receive Them
subtitle: 2 John 1:7–13
description: Deceivers gone out who refuse the flesh-confession, a door closed to the teacher who does not bring the teaching, and a close that hopes for face to face over paper and ink.
paragraphs: The warning names its cause first. “For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.” Gone out into the world: the deceivers are travelers, moving between households like the teachers of that age moved, carrying a teaching. Their mark is a refusal, the confession they will not make, the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh, worded here as a coming where the long letter worded it as having come; the telling carries his wording as written and does not harmonize the two. The verdict is total, the deceiver and the antichrist, and it is carried at the strength he states it, with no person or movement of any later age named or aimed at.

Against that traffic the first instruction is aimed at the household itself, not at the deceivers: “Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded.” Watch yourselves. The danger is loss, of work already done, we have worked for, the elder counting his own labor among theirs, and the aim is not bare survival but a full reward. A household can lose ground it already holds; that is the premise of the whole warning, and it is why an old commandment and a settled truth still need an elder's page.

The line itself is drawn at remaining. “Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.” Runs ahead is the picture: movement that feels like progress, out past the teaching, is graded as loss of God himself, while remaining, the least dramatic verb in the letter, carries the largest possession, both the Father and the Son. The telling builds no system on the verse in either direction. It stands as he writes it, a test with two outcomes and no third.

Then the instruction reaches the front door, and it is carried at full strength in its own setting: “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him.” “Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.” In a world where traveling teachers lived on household hospitality, receiving a man into the home was receiving his teaching into the house church's life, and a greeting was fellowship's public handshake. The elder closes both to the teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ, and calls even the greeting a sharing in evil deeds. The telling constructs no modern application from it, neither widening it into a rule for every relationship nor softening what he actually told her; it stands as his instruction to this household about the teachers at its door.

The page ends more gently than it warned. “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete.” Paper and ink have carried the warning; the rest he wants to say in person, and the hope is stated as his hope with no visit invented beyond it. Joy complete is the long letter's opening language come back at the close of the short one. And the last line is a greeting passed along, unexplained as he leaves it: “The children of your elect sister send you greetings.” With that, the elder's page is done, and the undated group has two letters left: one to a beloved friend named Gaius, and one with no address at all, from Jude.
